title: SR&ED Third-Party Payments - Canadian Tax Credit Glossary
description: Explore our Canadian SR&ED glossary to learn when SR&ED Third-Party Payments to universities or research institutes qualify for tax credits.
summary: SR&ED third-party payments are amounts a taxpayer pays to approved Canadian universities, colleges, research institutes or non-profit SR&ED corporations for SR&ED related to its business. Under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(ii) and (iii) of Canada's Income Tax Act, these payments count at 80% for investment tax credit purposes, and Form T1263 must be filed for each payment.

body.text: SR&ED third-party payments are amounts a taxpayer pays to approved Canadian universities, colleges, research institutes or non-profit SR&ED corporations for SR&ED related to its business. Under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(ii) and (iii) of Canada's Income Tax Act, these payments count at 80% for investment tax credit purposes, and Form T1263 must be filed for each payment.
Executive Summary and Statutory Baseline

Canada operates one of the most comprehensive fiscal incentive architectures for industrial innovation in the developed world, anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program.

The Canadian R&D tax landscape has undergone its most significant structural transformation in over a decade between December 2024 and March 2026. At the federal level, the enactment of Bill C-15, the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, fundamentally expanded the parameters of the SR&ED program retroactively for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. These legislative amendments doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3 million to $6 million (increasing the maximum annual cash refund from $1.05 million to $2.1 million), raised the taxable capital phase-out thresholds from the historic $10 million to $50 million band to a wider $15 million to $75 million corridor, introduced an alternative gross revenue phase-out election for Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs), extended the 35% enhanced refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and restored the eligibility of capital expenditures and capital lease costs after a ten-year hiatus.

Concurrently, at the provincial level, the Québec March 2025 Budget enacted a sweeping consolidation of provincial innovation incentives for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025. Québec abolished its fragmented legacy suite of R&D salary, university contract, pre-competitive partnership, and consortium tax credits, replacing them with the unified, fully refundable Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation (CRIC; designated by Revenu Québec as the crédit d'impôt pour la R-D et la précommercialisation), which provides a 30% credit on the first $1 million of eligible R&D and pre-commercialisation expenditures (including capital equipment) above an exclusion threshold, and 20% thereafter. Furthermore, for fiscal years commencing after December 31, 2025, Québec replaced its longstanding e-business information technology salary credit (CDAE) with the artificial-intelligence-focused CDAEIA credit.

body.text: Despite this legislative expansion of expenditure caps and eligible entity classes, technical audit enforcement by the CRA and judicial scrutiny by the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) remain exceptionally rigorous. Recent appellate decisions, culminating in Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada (2021 FCA 88) and Tuna Temple Inc. v. The King (2026 FCA 175), confirm that the five conjunctive criteria articulated by Justice Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen ([1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520) constitute mandatory statutory requirements rather than mere administrative guidelines. Claimants that misapply outdated regulatory parameters—such as claiming the pre-2013 65% prescribed proxy overhead rate instead of the statutory 55% rate under Regulation 2900(4), improperly claiming cloud computing expenditures under the proxy method, or missing the absolute 18-month reporting deadline under subsection 37(11)—face automatic assessment adjustments or complete forfeiture of statutory entitlements.
Federal Legislative Framework and the 2024–2026 Structural Reforms
Statutory Architecture of the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations

The federal SR&ED program is codified within the Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) (ITA) and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945) (ITR). Unlike discretionary grant mechanisms that depend on annual departmental budget allocations and competitive review committees, the SR&ED regime is a statutory entitlement structured around a two-pronged fiscal mechanism: the Section 37 cumulative income deduction pool and the Section 127 and Section 127.1 Investment Tax Credit regime.

Under the first prong, subsection 37(1) of the ITA permits a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada to deduct current expenditures (under paragraph 37(1)(a)) and newly restored capital expenditures (under paragraph 37(1)(b)) incurred in Canada on SR&ED directly related to a business of the taxpayer. Rather than expiring at year-end like ordinary operating deductions, undeducted Section 37 expenditures accumulate in a perpetual pool that can be deducted in full or in part in the current taxation year or carried forward indefinitely to offset business income in any subsequent taxation year. By contrast, subsection 37(2) governs current expenditures for SR&ED carried on outside Canada; while deductible in computing current-year business income, subsection 37(2) expenditures do not enter the perpetual Section 37 pool and do not qualify for Investment Tax Credits under Section 127, subject only to the narrow 10% foreign salary exception codified in subsection 37(1.5). Subsection 37(8) establishes the statutory rules linking specific expenditure categories to subsections 37(1) and 37(2), with paragraph 37(8)(d) defining expenditures of a current nature.

Under the second prong, Section 127 of the ITA permits a taxpayer to deduct an Investment Tax Credit from Part I tax otherwise payable, while Section 127.1 governs the refundability of unused credits. Subsection 127(9) defines the foundational statutory concepts of "investment tax credit", "qualified expenditure", and "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool". Pursuant to subsection 127(5), non-refundable SR&ED ITCs that cannot be utilised against Part I tax in the taxation year in which they are earned may be carried back three taxation years or carried forward up to 20 taxation years, provided that an ITC can only be carried back if it cannot be deducted in the year earned. Crucially, under the anti-double-dipping mechanics of subsections 13(7.1), 37(1), and 127(5), any SR&ED ITC claimed by a taxpayer in a given taxation year—whether applied to reduce Part I tax payable or received as a cash refund under Section 127.1—triggers a mandatory dollar-for-dollar reduction of the taxpayer's Section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool in the immediately following taxation year, which must be reported on Line 435 of Form T661. Furthermore, the ITA explicitly prohibits a corporation from claiming an SR&ED ITC on any expense or expenditure incurred in the course of earning income if any portion of that income is exempt income or is exempt from tax under Part I of the Act.

The operational bridge between the broad statutory provisions of the ITA and granular accounting compliance is contained in Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations. Specifically, Section 2900 of the ITR defines the prescribed proxy amount and establishes the salary base caps for specified employees, whereas Section 2902 enumerates "prescribed expenditures" (such as under paragraph 2902(b)) that are statutorily excluded from the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9) of the Act, even where those outlays remain deductible as ordinary business expenses.
Enactment of Bill C-15 and Expansion of the Enhanced Credit Regime

Prior to the 2024–2026 legislative cycle, the enhanced 35% refundable SR&ED ITC under subsection 127(10.1) was restricted exclusively to qualifying Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) on a maximum annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000 (yielding a maximum refundable credit of $1,050,000), which phased out on a straight-line basis where the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC and its associated corporate group fell between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000. While initial legislative draft proposals released in December 2024 and August 2025 contemplated an intermediate expenditure limit of $4,500,000, the federal government expanded the reform in Budget 2025 and enacted the final statutory thresholds through Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026.

For all taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, the amended provisions of subsections 127(10.1) through 127(10.64) and Section 127.1 establish a substantially broadened regime. First, the maximum annual SR&ED expenditure limit eligible for the enhanced 35% ITC—composed of the 15% basic ITC plus the 20% additional ITC under subsection 127(10.1)—is doubled from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000. Consequently, the maximum annual refundable cash credit on current expenditures doubles from $1,050,000 to $2,100,000 per taxation year. Second, under amended subsection 127(10.2), the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada phase-out thresholds for CCPCs and associated corporate groups are increased from $10,000,000 (lower threshold) and $50,000,000 (upper threshold) to $15,000,000 and $75,000,000, respectively. In addition, CCPCs and associated groups are granted an explicit statutory election to have their annual expenditure limit determined based on gross revenue rather than taxable capital employed in Canada; where this election is made for a taxation year, the expenditure limit phase-out based on taxable capital employed in Canada under subsection 127(10.2) ceases to apply to the corporate group for that year. Associated corporations must execute and file a valid allocation agreement under subsection 127(10.3) to apportion the shared $6,000,000 expenditure limit among group members before claiming the enhanced rate.

Third, and for the first time in the history of the SR&ED program, Canadian-resident public corporations that qualify as Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) (or consolidated ECPC groups, taking into account "consolidated financial statements" as defined in subsection 127(9)) under newly enacted subsections 127(10.6) and 127(10.64) (with former subsection 127(10.6) renumbered as subsection 127(10.5)) are entitled to claim the enhanced 35% refundable ITC up to the $6,000,000 annual expenditure limit. However, two critical statutory distinctions separate ECPCs from CCPCs in audit practice. Unlike a CCPC whose expenditure limit defaults to prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada, an ECPC's $6,000,000 expenditure limit is phased out between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000 based strictly on the corporation's (or consolidated group's) average gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years. Furthermore, whereas qualifying CCPCs may receive partial (40%) refundability on the 15% basic ITC earned on current expenditures exceeding their annual expenditure limit, any qualifying expenditures incurred by an ECPC in excess of its annual expenditure limit earn the 15% basic ITC on a strictly non-refundable basis.

Once X reaches or exceeds $75,000,000, the expenditure limit is reduced to nil, and all qualified expenditures earn the 15% non-refundable basic ITC.
Restoration of Capital Expenditures and Lease Costs

Between January 1, 2014, and December 15, 2024, capital expenditures—including capital lease payments and historical shared-use equipment—were completely excluded from both the Section 37 deduction pool and Section 127 qualified expenditures. Effective for depreciable property acquired on or after December 16, 2024, and, in the case of lease costs, amounts that first become payable on or after December 16, 2024, subsection 37(1) is amended via the addition of paragraph 37(1)(b) and subsection 127(9) is amended to restore full SR&ED eligibility for capital expenditures.

To qualify under the restored capital rules, the acquired depreciable property must satisfy strict statutory conditions regarding timing, usage intensity, and overhead elections. Specifically, the capital property must be acquired on or after December 16, 2024, and cannot be included in the Section 37 pool or Section 127 qualified expenditures until it satisfies the statutory "available for use" rules in the taxation year. Furthermore, capital equipment must be intended to be used all or substantially all—defined administratively and judicially as 90% or more of its operating time over its useful life—for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. With respect to leased equipment where lease costs first become payable on or after December 16, 2024, 100% of the lease cost qualifies if the equipment is used 90% or more for SR&ED in Canada; if the claimant elects the proxy overhead method and the leased equipment is used primarily (more than 50%, up to 90%) for SR&ED in Canada, 50% of the lease cost qualifies as an SR&ED expenditure. Under the proxy method, general office equipment and furniture remain prescribed expenditures under Regulation 2902 and are ineligible.

Crucially, the refundability profile of capital SR&ED expenditures diverges from that of current SR&ED expenditures. Under amended Section 127.1, while a qualifying CCPC receives a 100% refund of the 35% enhanced ITC on current SR&ED expenditures within its expenditure limit (including under subsection 127.1(2.01) for a CCPC that is neither a qualifying corporation nor an excluded corporation as defined in subsection 127.1(2)), the statutory rate of refundability for the 35% ITC earned on capital SR&ED expenditures and eligible lease costs is fixed at 40%. This mechanism yields a 14% immediate cash refund (40% × 35%) on capital property acquired within the expenditure limit, with the remaining 60% of the credit (representing 21% of the capital cost) retained as a non-refundable ITC available to offset Part I tax payable or be carried back 3 years and forward 20 years.
Technical Eligibility Criteria and Judicial Precedents
The Subsection 248(1) Definition and Excluded Commercial Activities

Whether an industrial or scientific activity constitutes SR&ED in Canadian law is governed exclusively by the statutory definition codified in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. Subsection 248(1) defines "scientific research and experimental development" as a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis and that falls within one of four qualifying statutory branches. Paragraph 248(1)(a) encompasses basic research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Paragraph 248(1)(b) encompasses applied research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Paragraph 248(1)(c)—under which the vast majority of Canadian commercial claims are filed—encompasses experimental development, defined as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Finally, paragraph 248(1)(d) permits the inclusion of support work with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, but strictly on the condition that such work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development described in paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer.

Immediately following paragraph (d), subsection 248(1) enumerates seven categorical exclusions in paragraphs (e) through (k) that demarcate the boundary between eligible R&D and routine commercial operations. Even where an activity requires advanced professional skill or complex engineering, it is statutorily excluded from SR&ED if it is work with respect to market research or sales promotion under paragraph (e); quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes under paragraph (f); research in the social sciences or the humanities under paragraph (g); prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas under paragraph (h); the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process under paragraph (i); style changes under paragraph (j); or routine data collection under paragraph (k).

In administrative practice, the CRA's updated Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives guidelines distil the subsection 248(1) definition into two overarching pedagogical requirements: the "Why" requirement (whether the work was conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement) and the "How" requirement (whether the work was a systematic investigation or search carried out by means of experiment or analysis). However, as the CRA explicitly acknowledges in its historical guidance notes and as the Tax Court of Canada repeatedly holds, both the two administrative requirements ("Why" and "How") and the five judicial questions are derived directly from subsection 248(1) of the ITA, which has not changed, and whenever any conflict arises between CRA administrative publications and the ITA as interpreted by the courts, the statute and judicial precedent strictly govern.
The Five-Criterion Judicial Test in Northwest Hydraulic and Appellate Affirmations

The foundational legal test for SR&ED eligibility in Canada was articulated by Justice Bowman (as he then was) of the Tax Court of Canada in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 D.T.C. 1839 (at paragraph 16). Although Justice Bowman noted at paragraph 15 that the CRA's Information Circular 86-4R3 (dated May 24, 1994) served as a "generally useful and reliable guide", he formulated five distinct legal criteria to govern statutory interpretation under the principle that the provision be given such fair, large, and liberal interpretation as best ensures the attainment of its objects. The Federal Court of Appeal subsequently adopted and codified Justice Bowman's five criteria as binding national law in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, [1999] 1 C.T.C. 132, 99 D.T.C. 5087 (FCA) (at paragraph 10), and summarized them in canonical form in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393 (at paragraph 17).

Under the first criterion, the court asks whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. Standard procedures and routine engineering refer to techniques, procedures, and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field. If the resolution of a technical problem is reasonably predictable using established engineering methodologies or publicly available technical documentation, no technological uncertainty exists. Under the second criterion, the court asks whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty. Justice Bowman established that this second criterion requires a structured five-stage process comprising: (a) the observation of the subject matter of the problem; (b) the formulation of a clear objective; (c) the identification and articulation of the technological uncertainty; (d) the formulation of a hypothesis or hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate the uncertainty; and (e) the methodical and systematic testing of the hypotheses. As further interpreted by the Tax Court in Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6, and applied in Canafric Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 108, a qualifying hypothesis must be a testable proposition explaining a causal scientific or technological relationship, rather than a mere commercial goal or intuitive guess.

Under the third criterion, the court evaluates whether the procedure adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses. The investigation must follow a logical progression where the results of each experiment or analysis are evaluated against the hypothesis and used to modify subsequent hypotheses systematically. Under the fourth criterion, the court determines whether the process resulted in a technological advancement. In a business context, when a new or improved product or process is created, it must embody a scientific or technological advancement—generating new knowledge that advances the understanding of scientific relations or technologies beyond the existing state of the art. Finally, under the fifth criterion, the court examines whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and results was kept as the work progressed.

In Lehigh Hanson Materials Limited v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 205 (at paragraph 37), and reaffirmed in Anne-Marie Chagnon Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 35 (per Justice Guy R. Smith) as well as Zeuter Development Corp. v. Her Majesty the Queen and Dock Edge Inc., the Tax Court emphasized that to be eligible for SR&ED, each of the five questions in the five-factor test must be answered in the affirmative. Because the judicial test is strictly conjunctive, a taxpayer's failure to satisfy any single criterion is fatal to the entire SR&ED claim.

Taxpayers have repeatedly attempted to challenge the third criterion (accordance with the "scientific method") by arguing that after Northwest Hydraulic was decided, the statutory definition of SR&ED was moved from the Income Tax Regulations to subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, and that the statutory text does not explicitly contain the phrase "scientific method". In Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88 (Docket A-442-19, decided May 10, 2021, per Justice Wyman W. Webb), the Federal Court of Appeal decisively rejected this argument and dismissed the taxpayer's appeal with costs. Justice Webb held that Justice Bowman was directly interpreting the statutory definition of SR&ED ("systematic investigation or search... by means of experiment or analysis"), that the statutory definition in subsection 248(1) is not materially different from the former regulatory definition, and that an unbroken line of Federal Court of Appeal decisions—including RIS-Christie (1998), C.W. Agencies (2001), Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen (2011 FCA 355, at paragraph 6), and R&D Pro-Innovation Inc. v. Canada (2016 FCA 152, at paragraph 4)—binds the Tax Court to apply all five Northwest Hydraulic criteria.
Contemporaneous Documentation, Software Trial-and-Error, and Recent Jurisprudence

The interplay between the third criterion (systematic investigation) and the fifth criterion (contemporaneous record-keeping) represents the primary battleground in Canadian SR&ED audits and Tax Court litigation. In RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, [1999] 1 C.T.C. 132 (at paragraphs 14 and 15), the Federal Court of Appeal clarified the legal nature of the fifth criterion: while Justice Bowman stated in Northwest Hydraulic that a detailed record of hypotheses, tests, and results must be kept as the work progresses, the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations do not contain an explicit statutory mandate requiring that evidence be exclusively documentary. Consequently, as confirmed by the Tax Court in Formadrain Inc. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 42, at paragraph 118), Les Abeilles (at paragraph 94), and National R&D Inc. v. The Queen (2020 TCC 47, at paragraphs 65 and 66), testimonial evidence is legally admissible to establish that SR&ED took place. However, the courts consistently warn that relying on oral testimony without contemporaneous documentation carries severe evidentiary risk, because human recollection rarely suffices to prove the precise formulation of hypotheses, quantitative test parameters, and sequential modifications over multi-year development cycles.

This evidentiary hazard is vividly illustrated in National R&D Inc. v. The Queen, 2020 TCC 47 (Court File No. 2017-3837(IT)G, decided July 7, 2020, per Justice Dominique Lafleur; aff'd 2022 FCA 72, leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada dismissed March 9, 2023). The appellant sought SR&ED credits for its 2011 taxation year regarding the "PTS Project", a computer program designed to automate time-tracking and filing of SR&ED claims with the CRA at a time when web-based tools such as QuickBooks Online had limited functionality. Although the principal witness, Mr. Saini, testified that he took contemporaneous notes while coding the PTS Project, Justice Lafleur dismissed the appeal with costs, finding that the appellant failed to demonstrate a "logical progression between each test and preceding or subsequent tests" and therefore failed to prove that a systematic investigation was carried out. In software engineering and data analytics claims, coding by trial-and-error, iterative debugging, or integrating existing frameworks without a documented, logical progression of hypothesis formulation and experimental verification fails the third criterion of Northwest Hydraulic.

Similarly, in 6379249 Canada Inc. v. The Queen (2015 TCC, Docket 2012-3634), the Tax Court examined a Montreal-based appellant developing a miniature mobile device with integrated printing capabilities and touch screens manufactured in Montreal and shipped to China and India. For the 2006 and 2007 taxation years, the CRA's National Technology Sector Specialist and Research and Technology Advisor (RTA), Mr. Wierzbica, accepted that the development of the miniature printer constituted eligible SR&ED because no publicly available technical information existed at the time to guide engineers on building such a small device with printing capability. However, for the 2009 and 2010 taxation years, after the printer had been commercially released and sent to manufacturing, subsequent work aimed at determining why the manufactured printers did not consistently meet specifications was denied. The Court upheld the denial for 2009 and 2010, noting the RTA's testimony that once the product was released to commercial manufacturing (excluded under paragraph 248(1)(i)), post-release troubleshooting where each activity viewed separately constituted standard engineering did not qualify as SR&ED.

Most recently, in Tuna Temple Inc. v. The King, 2026 FCA 175, the Federal Court of Appeal reaffirmed the strict application of Northwest Hydraulic and RIS-Christie, upholding the Tax Court's dismissal (2025 TCC 183) of an SR&ED appeal where the claimant lacked systematic, contemporaneous records linking experimental tests to underlying technological uncertainties.

body.text: Qualifying Expenditures, Overhead Methodologies, and Anti-Duplication Rules
Salaries, Wages, and Specified Employee Limitations

Direct labour typically comprises the largest expenditure component of a Canadian SR&ED claim. Under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) and subsection 127(9) of the ITA, a taxpayer may include 100% of the portion of salaries and wages paid to employees for the time they are directly engaged in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, encompassing hands-on technical experimentation, eligible paragraph 248(1)(d) support work, and first-line technical supervision.

Three strict statutory constraints govern the inclusion of salaries and wages in an SR&ED claim. First, remuneration paid to shareholder-founders in the form of corporate dividends does not constitute salary or wages and adds nothing to the Section 37 deduction pool, the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool, or the proxy salary base. While paying salary requires the corporation and founder to remit Canada Pension Plan (CPP) contributions and payroll source deductions, only T4 salary generates eligible SR&ED base and the accompanying 55% overhead proxy uplift. Second, under subsection 37(1.5) of the ITA, salaries and wages for SR&ED work performed outside Canada are eligible for inclusion in the subsection 37(1) pool and Section 127 ITCs only where the employee is resident in Canada, the foreign work is performed solely in support of SR&ED carried on by the taxpayer in Canada, and the total foreign salary claimed does not exceed 10% of the total eligible SR&ED salaries and wages paid for SR&ED carried on in Canada during the taxation year.

Third, the Income Tax Regulations impose rigorous anti-avoidance caps on "specified employees"—defined as employees who are specified shareholders owning, directly or indirectly, at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation, or who do not deal at arm's length with the corporation. For specified employees, bonuses and remuneration based on profits are strictly excluded from eligible SR&ED salaries under paragraph 37(9)(a) of the ITA, and the direct SR&ED salary claimable for a specified employee is capped under subsection 37(9.1) at five times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE), prorated for the number of days in the taxation year that the individual is a specified employee. Furthermore, under subsection 2900(7) of the ITR, when computing the salary base to which the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount applies, the includable salary of a specified employee is capped at the lesser of 75% of the employee's salary or wages for the year and 2.5 times the YMPE (prorated by days of employment), and subsection 2900(8) applies the 2.5 × YMPE cap on an aggregate basis where associated corporations employ the same specified employee; under subsection 2900(9), bonuses, remuneration based on profits, and taxable benefits are excluded from the proxy salary base.
The Prescribed Proxy Amount versus the Traditional Overhead Method

To account for overhead and other expenditures directly attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED, a taxpayer must make an annual election on Line 160 in Part 3 of Form T661 to use either the Proxy Method or the Traditional Method. Under Section 37 of the ITA, this election must be made on the first Form T661 filed for the taxation year and is irrevocable for that taxation year once submitted.

Under the Proxy Method, the taxpayer does not specifically identify, track, or claim actual SR&ED overhead expenditures on Form T661. Instead, the taxpayer calculates a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations equal to 55% of the eligible SR&ED salary base of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada. A frequent technical error observed in some advisory literature is the citation of a 65% proxy rate for 2026 filings. Regulatory history confirms that the PPA rate was 65% only for taxation years ending in 2012 and earlier, dropped to 60% for 2013, and has been fixed at 55% since 2014 under Regulation 2900(4). Overstating the proxy rate by ten percentage points results in an immediate assessment correction on every claim. Moreover, the salary base to which the 55% PPA applies is narrower than total SR&ED payroll: bonuses, profit-based remuneration, and taxable benefits are excluded for all employees, and specified employees are subject to the subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8) caps. Because the PPA is a notional amount defined in paragraph (b) of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9), it earns the Section 127 ITC but is not added to the Section 37 deduction pool, and it cannot exceed the corporation's total eligible overhead-type business expenses incurred for the year. For example, if an Ontario software CCPC pays its developers $400,000 in base salary and time records substantiate that 75% of their hours were devoted to eligible SR&ED ($300,000), the 55% proxy adds $165,000 in notional overhead (assuming total corporate overhead exceeds the proxy cap), producing $465,000 in qualified expenditures.

Conversely, under the Traditional Method, the taxpayer receives no notional proxy uplift and must instead itemise, track, and substantiate actual overhead and other expenditures that are directly related to the prosecution of SR&ED and incremental—meaning they would not have been incurred but for the SR&ED work. Actual overhead claimed under the Traditional Method is added to both the Section 37 deduction pool and the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool. Crucially, CRA policy classifies cloud computing expenses, server hosting fees, and software subscriptions used in R&D environments as overhead expenditures. Contrary to common misconceptions, cloud and subscription costs cannot be claimed under the Proxy Method because the 55% PPA stands in for all overhead expenses; a cloud invoice can only be claimed if the taxpayer elects the Traditional Method. Consequently, the choice between the Proxy Method and the Traditional Method is an arithmetic optimization: for a team of five engineers earning $600,000 in eligible SR&ED salary, the 55% proxy generates $330,000 of notional overhead with minimal record-keeping, making the Proxy Method superior unless the company's incremental cloud compute and infrastructure spend exceeds $330,000 (55% of the salary base).

body.text: Subcontractors, Third-Party Payments, and Materials Consumed or Transformed

Beyond direct labour and overhead, three additional expenditure categories enter the SR&ED calculation: materials, arm's-length and non-arm's-length subcontractor payments, and third-party institutional payments. A taxpayer may include 100% of the cost of materials that are either consumed (rendered virtually valueless or destroyed during testing) or transformed (integrated into an experimental prototype or pilot plant) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.

With respect to contractor expenditures under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.01) and (i.1), payments made to arm's-length contractors who perform eligible SR&ED in Canada on behalf of the claimant are 100% deductible in the Section 37 pool, subject to the subsection 37(14) look-through rule ensuring that third-party payments include only expenditures of a current nature. However, under subparagraph (a)(ii) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9), only 80% of an arm's-length SR&ED contract expenditure qualifies for the Section 127 Investment Tax Credit. Crucially, the contracted SR&ED work must be performed physically within Canada; any offshore portion performed outside Canada does not qualify. Where an SR&ED contract is entered into with a non-arm's-length party, the contract payment earns no ITC of its own for the payer; instead, the non-arm's-length performer may claim its own underlying expenditures, or the parties may file Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) under subsection 127(13) of the ITA to transfer the qualified expenditures to the payer. Similarly, third-party payments under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(ii) and (iii) to approved Canadian universities, colleges, research institutes, or non-profit SR&ED corporations for SR&ED related to the taxpayer's business are included at 80% for ITC purposes under subsection 127(9) and require the filing of Form T1263 for each payment.
Government Assistance, Non-Government Assistance, and Contract Payment Reductions

A foundational rule of Canadian R&D tax law is that a claimant may earn SR&ED tax incentives only on its net out-of-pocket expenditure. Under subsection 127(11.1) and paragraph 37(1)(d) of the ITA—not subsection 37(2), which deals exclusively with foreign SR&ED—any government assistance or non-government assistance that a taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive in respect of SR&ED reduces both the qualified expenditure pool and the Section 37 deduction pool dollar for dollar. Government assistance is broadly defined in subsection 127(9) to encompass any grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, or investment allowance from a government, municipality, or other public authority. This includes direct federal grants—such as cost-shared R&D contributions from the National Research Council Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP), wage subsidies under the Student Work Placement Program (SWPP), digital adoption grants under the Ontario Centre of Innovation Digital Modernization and Adoption Plan (OCI DMAP), and interest-free contributions up to 50% ($125,000 to $5,000,000) under FedDev Ontario's Regional AI Initiative—as well as all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits. Non-government assistance, including commercial forgivable loans or private inducements, triggers the exact same dollar-for-dollar reduction under subsection 127(11.1).

Similarly, to prevent duplicate SR&ED claims by both a client payer and a performing contractor on the same R&D project in Canada, subsections 127(18) to 127(20) of the ITA require a contractor to reduce its qualified expenditures by the gross amount of any "contract payment"—defined as an amount payable for SR&ED performed for or on behalf of a person or partnership entitled to a deduction under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) or (i.1) at arm's length, or payable by a Canadian government, municipality, public authority, or tax-exempt entity under Section 149.
Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

Every Canadian province and territory except Prince Edward Island, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut provides a statutory R&D income tax credit that stacks alongside the federal SR&ED credit. While Prince Edward Island lacks a statutory corporate income tax credit, it operates the Innovation and Development Labour Rebate, which rebates up to 25% of eligible R&D labour costs. Among the ten jurisdictions offering statutory R&D tax credits, eight (Ontario, British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, and Yukon) harmonize their definitions of eligible SR&ED with subsection 248(1) of the federal ITA and delegate administration to the CRA via T2 corporate tax schedules, whereas Québec (administered by Revenu Québec and Investissement Québec) and Alberta (administered by Alberta Treasury Board and Finance) maintain independent provincial tax administration regimes.
Ontario R&D Tax Incentives (OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC)

Corporations maintaining a permanent establishment in Ontario and performing eligible SR&ED within the province can simultaneously stack up to three statutory R&D tax credits administered by the CRA since January 1, 2009, under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario). First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC), claimed on Schedule T2SCH566, provides a 100% refundable tax credit equal to 8% of qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures up to an annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000 for taxation years commencing after May 31, 2016 (having been reduced from 10% for taxation years ending before June 1, 2016). Although the 2018–19 Ontario Budget proposed an R&D-intensity-based graduated OITC rate ranging between 8% and 12%, that proposal was not enacted following a change in provincial government, leaving the flat 8% refundable rate in force. Any OITC in excess of Ontario tax otherwise payable is refunded in cash without carryback or carryforward provisions, and no recapture applies, though the OITC reduces the federal pool of deductible and qualified SR&ED expenditures unless waived by the company.

Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC), codified in Sections 38 to 45 of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) and claimed on Schedule T2SCH508 alongside federal Schedule T2SCH31, provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit on all eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures for taxation years starting after May 31, 2016 (reduced from 4.5% prior to June 1, 2016). Unused ORDTC can be carried back 3 years (to tax years ending on or after January 1, 2009) and carried forward 20 years to reduce Ontario corporate income tax payable, and recapture applies. Because the ORDTC constitutes government assistance that reduces the federal SR&ED qualified expenditure pool under ITA subsection 127(11.1), a corporation with no Ontario tax payable can formally waive the ORDTC (or a portion thereof) by delivering a written waiver with its T2 return within six months of its tax year-end, or on an amended return for that year, thereby preserving its 35% refundable federal SR&ED credit.

Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC), claimed on Schedule T2SCH568, provides a 20% fully refundable tax credit to corporations (and corporate partners other than specified members) on up to $20,000,000 per associated group in qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in Ontario under eligible contracts with approved Eligible Research Institutes (ERIs), excluding any expenditure funding salaries of ERI employees connected to the claimant corporation. Alongside these three SR&ED credits, Ontario firms frequently utilize the Ontario Interactive Digital Media Tax Credit (OIDMTC, offering up to a 40% refundable credit on interactive digital media and gaming labour costs) and the Ontario Made Manufacturing Investment Tax Credit (OMMITC, enhanced in Budget 2025 to up to 15% refundable on eligible manufacturing buildings and equipment).
Québec's 2025–2026 Consolidation: From Legacy Payroll Credits to the CRIC and CDAEIA

Québec has historically maintained the most multifaceted provincial R&D tax credit system in Canada, administered by Revenu Québec and Investissement Québec against a provincial corporate tax backdrop where the small-business tax rate is 3.20% (12.20% combined with federal) and the general corporate tax rate is 11.50% (26.50% combined). In its March 25, 2025 Budget, the Québec government enacted a landmark structural reform that replaced its legacy multi-credit R&D payroll and contract system with a unified regime for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025.

For taxation years beginning on or before March 25, 2025, claimants continue to apply Québec's former suite of refundable R&D tax credits. Under the legacy regime, the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) (Form RD-1029.7) provided a 100% refundable credit of 30% for qualifying SMEs (corporations with assets under $50,000,000) and 14% for large businesses on 100% of Quebec R&D salaries and 50% of subcontractor contracts, subject to an exclusion threshold between $50,000 (for SMEs) and $225,000 (for large businesses). The legacy regime also featured specialized credits—all abolished for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025—including the tax credit for university research or research carried on by a public research centre or research consortium (Form RD-1029.8.6, paying 30% SME / 14% large on 80% of contracts), the tax credit for private partnership pre-competitive research (Form RD-1029.8.16.1, paying 30% SME / 14% large on 100% of current expenses and 80% of subcontracts), the tax credit for fees and dues paid to a research consortium (Form RD-1029.8.9.03, paying 30% SME / 14% large on 100% of dues, with transitional carryforward rules allowing an eligible fee balance at the end of a tax year ending after March 25, 2025, to be claimed for tax years ending on or before December 31, 2029), the tax credit for technological adaptation services, and the industrial design component of the in-house design credit (formerly 24% SME / 12% large, whereas the fashion design component remains in force).

For all taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, those abolished credits are consolidated into the Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation (CRIC). The CRIC expands Québec's qualifying base to cover both R&D and pre-commercialisation expenditures carried out in Québec, and restores capital equipment expenditures to the provincial R&D credit base. (To support collaborative research under the CRIC, the Act respecting the sectoral parameters of certain fiscal measures was amended so the Minister of the Economy, Innovation and Energy continues to issue recognition certificates for eligible public research centres and eligible research consortia). The CRIC is 100% refundable and pays 30% on the first $1,000,000 of eligible R&D and pre-commercialisation spending above the statutory exclusion threshold, and 20% on all eligible spending above $1,000,000. Corporations claim the CRIC with Revenu Québec by filing Form RD-1029.8.CR-T alongside their CO-17 corporate tax return within 18 months of their fiscal year-end.

In parallel, Québec restructured its flagship software and IT payroll incentive. For fiscal years starting in 2025, the Crédit d'impôt pour le développement des affaires électroniques (CDAE) provides a 30% credit (split into 23% refundable and 7% non-refundable, compared to 24% refundable and 6% non-refundable in 2024) on eligible IT employee salaries capped at $83,333 per employee where the employee spends at least 75% of their time on eligible activities. Effective for fiscal years starting after December 31, 2025, the CDAE is replaced by the CDAEIA (Crédit d'impôt pour le développement des affaires électroniques intégrant l'intelligence artificielle), which requires an annual certificate from Investissement Québec confirming that the corporation integrates artificial intelligence features in a significant way, and applies above an exclusion threshold until December 31, 2030.

body.text: Beyond the CRIC and CDAEIA, innovative corporations in Québec can access the multimedia title tax credit (CDTIM, paying up to 37.5% on eligible labour with an Investissement Québec certificate), the investment and innovation tax credit (C3i, paying 15%, 20%, or 25% fully refundable by region on manufacturing equipment, computer hardware, and management software costs above $5,000 or $12,500 per property up to a $100,000,000 four-year cumulative cap), and the incentive deduction for the commercialisation of innovations in Québec (IDCI, which taxes qualifying Québec intellectual property income at an effective corporate rate of 2.0% instead of the general 11.5% rate). Early-stage and sector-specific Québec innovators also frequently stack direct grants such as Programme Innovation — Primo-Adoptants ($10,000 to $75,000 for pre-commercial startups under 5 years old), CQDM SynergiQC (up to $1,500,000 over 3 years for life-sciences R&D), Technoclimat (up to $18,000,000 subject to a 75% combined-government cap), and IVADO Scientist in Action AI intern grants ($3,750 to $11,250).
Western Provinces: British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba

Across Western Canada, all four provinces maintain statutory R&D incentives tailored to their industrial bases. In British Columbia, the BC SR&ED Tax Credit (claimed on Form T666 and administered by the CRA) provides a 10% refundable tax credit to qualifying CCPCs (and, for tax years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, eligible Canadian public corporations) on eligible BC SR&ED expenditures up to their expenditure limit (increased to $6,000,000 for those tax years), and a 10% non-refundable tax credit on expenditures exceeding the expenditure limit or incurred by other corporations.

In Alberta, the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG)—enacted for eligible R&D expenditures incurred after December 31, 2020, and administered independently by Alberta Treasury Board and Finance via Form AT1 Schedule 29—provides a 100% refundable payment on up to $4,000,000 of annual eligible SR&ED expenditures carried out in Alberta. The IEG operates on a two-tier incremental formula: it pays an 8% base payment on eligible Alberta R&D spending up to the corporation's base level of spending (defined as the corporation's average eligible Alberta R&D spending over the preceding two taxation years) and an enhanced 20% payment (8% base plus 12% incremental bonus) on eligible R&D spending that exceeds the two-year average base spending level.

In Saskatchewan, the Saskatchewan R&D Tax Credit (claimed on Schedule T2SCH403 and administered by the CRA) provides a 10% tax credit on eligible Saskatchewan SR&ED expenditures (reduced from 15% for expenditures incurred after March 31, 2015). Since April 1, 2017, the 10% credit is refundable for CCPCs on the first $1,000,000 of qualifying expenditures each year (yielding up to $100,000 in refundable cash) and non-refundable on amounts above $1,000,000 and for non-CCPCs.

In Manitoba, the Manitoba R&D Tax Credit (claimed on Schedule T2SCH380 and administered by the CRA) provides a 15% tax credit on eligible SR&ED expenditures made in Manitoba after April 11, 2017 (reduced from 20% prior to April 12, 2017). For in-house R&D conducted by a corporation, one-half (50%) of the 15% credit is refundable (yielding a 7.5% refundable credit) and the remaining 7.5% is non-refundable, whereas eligible R&D conducted under a contract with a qualifying post-secondary or research institution in Manitoba earns the full 15% credit on a refundable basis. Manitoba also offers a refundable Interactive Digital Media Tax Credit of up to 40% on eligible labour and marketing expenses.
Atlantic Provinces and Northern Territories

In Atlantic Canada and the Northern Territories, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, and Yukon each provide a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit administered by the CRA with no annual expenditure cap. In Nova Scotia, Section 41 of the Income Tax Act (Nova Scotia) provides a 15% fully refundable credit (claimed on Schedule T2SCH340 within 18 months of the corporation's tax year-end) to corporations with a permanent establishment in Nova Scotia; recapture applies, and a corporation may renounce the credit on or before six months after its tax year-end. Nova Scotia also provides a refundable Interactive Digital Media Tax Credit of up to 50% on eligible labour expenses or 25% on total eligible expenses. In New Brunswick, corporations with a permanent establishment in the province claim a 15% fully refundable credit on Schedule T2SCH360.

In Newfoundland and Labrador, Section 42 of the Income Tax Act (Newfoundland and Labrador) provides a 15% fully refundable credit (claimed on Schedule T2SCH301 within 12 months after the filing-due date) to corporations, individuals, trust beneficiaries, and partnership members with a permanent establishment in the province. Uniquely in Canada, Newfoundland and Labrador statutory rules specify that eligible provincial SR&ED expenditures are not reduced by government or non-government assistance (except GST/HST input tax credits), nor does recapture apply, although the resulting 15% NL credit still reduces the federal pool of deductible and qualified SR&ED expenditures. Newfoundland and Labrador also offers a refundable Interactive Digital Media Tax Credit of 40% on labour and 25% on other eligible costs (capped at $40,000 per employee and $2,000,000 per company). Finally, in Yukon, the Yukon R&D Tax Credit (claimed on Schedule T2SCH442 for corporations or Form T1232 for individuals) provides a 15% fully refundable credit on eligible SR&ED expenditures incurred in Yukon, plus an additional 5% refundable credit (20% total) on amounts paid or payable to Yukon University (formerly Yukon College).
Federal-Provincial Stacking Mechanics and Net Cash Recovery Modelling

A critical audit finding in Canadian R&D financial modelling is that federal and provincial tax credit rates do not simply add together linearly. Because every provincial or territorial R&D tax credit constitutes "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) and subsection 127(11.1) of the federal Income Tax Act, the provincial credit earned in a taxation year reduces the federal SR&ED qualified expenditure pool dollar-for-dollar before the 35% (or 15%) federal ITC rate is applied.

To illustrate the exact statutory stacking formula across jurisdictions, consider a qualifying CCPC within its $6,000,000 expenditure limit that elects the Proxy Method (55% PPA) and pays $100,000 in eligible direct SR&ED salary (with no bonuses, taxable benefits, or specified employee reductions). Adding the $55,000 Prescribed Proxy Amount to the $100,000 salary produces a gross federal qualified expenditure pool of $155,000. In provinces harmonized with the federal qualified expenditure definition (Ontario, British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, and Yukon), the provincial credit rate applies to the full $155,000 proxy-loaded base; in Québec under the CRIC, the 30% credit applies to actual eligible expenditures ($100,000 direct salary) without the federal notional proxy uplift. body.text: The comparative stacking analysis reveals a crucial second-order financial insight regarding Ontario's dual-credit architecture. If a pre-revenue or loss-making CCPC in Ontario claims both the 8% refundable OITC ($12,400) and the 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC ($4,991, computed on the $142,600 base remaining after the OITC reduction), the non-refundable $4,991 ORDTC reduces the corporation's federal qualified expenditure pool from $142,600 to $137,609, thereby reducing its immediate 35% federal cash refund by $1,747 (from $49,910 down to $48,163). By formally waiving the 3.5% ORDTC under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), a pre-profit startup increases its immediate cash recovery from 60.56% to 62.31% of direct SR&ED salary.
Administrative Governance, Compliance Procedures, and Audit Defence
Governing Authorities, Prescribed Tax Forms, and Statutory Filing Deadlines

The administration of R&D tax incentives in Canada is divided between federal and provincial tax and innovation authorities. The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) administers the federal SR&ED program and all harmonized provincial and territorial credits. Within the CRA's SR&ED Directorate, claims undergo a coordinated review by Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) (advised on complex files by National Technology Sector Specialists), who evaluate technical eligibility under subsection 248(1), and Financial Reviewers, who audit expenditure pools, overhead calculations, and specified employee restrictions. In Québec, Revenu Québec administers tax credit assessments and payouts via the CO-17 corporate return, while Investissement Québec (alongside the Ministère de l'Économie, de l'Innovation et de l'Énergie and the Ministère des Finances du Québec) issues mandatory technical eligibility certificates for the CDAEIA and CDTIM programs.

body.text: One of the strictest statutory compliance rules in Canadian tax law is the SR&ED reporting deadline codified in subsection 37(11) of the ITA (governing the Section 37 deduction pool) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) (governing Section 127 ITCs). Under these provisions, a claimant must submit Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 (or Form T2038(IND) for individuals) containing all prescribed information on or before the day that is 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year. Because a corporation's T2 return is due six months after the end of its taxation year under paragraph 150(1)(a) of the ITA, the statutory SR&ED filing window runs exactly 18 months from the end of the corporation's fiscal year. For example, a corporation with a December 31, 2025 fiscal year-end has a T2 filing-due date of June 30, 2026, and an absolute SR&ED reporting deadline of June 30, 2027; on July 1, 2027, the credit for that taxation year is permanently extinguished. If a taxpayer is amending Form T661 or Schedule T2SCH31 electronically, the amended forms must be submitted alongside an amended income tax return prior to the expiry of the 18-month deadline. The Income Tax Act contains no statutory mechanism or ministerial discretion to extend or waive this 18-month deadline. An identical 18-month filing deadline applies to Québec's CRIC (Form RD-1029.8.CR-T) and Nova Scotia's R&D tax credit (Schedule T2SCH340).
Pre-Claim Approval, CRA Technical and Financial Reviews, and Dispute Resolution

To provide upfront eligibility certainty before a claim is filed, the CRA offers an optional Pre-Claim Approval process (ideally requested before the R&D project begins) to corporations whose gross business income is under $25,000,000. While pre-claim approval confirms whether planned projects meet the subsection 248(1) definition of SR&ED, the corporation must still file Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 after year-end within the 18-month deadline.

When a filed claim is selected for audit by the CRA, the review is governed by the Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors and Appendix 2 of Guide T4088. The RTA scrutinizes the technical narrative in Part 2 of Form T661, where the claimant must articulate the technological uncertainties, the systematic experimentation or analysis conducted, and the resulting technological advancements. In accordance with RIS-Christie, National R&D, and Tuna Temple, RTAs expect contemporaneous documentation generated as the work progressed—such as time-tracking logs separating R&D from non-R&D hours, source code repositories, test logs, and engineering notes—rather than narratives reconstructed retroactively at year-end. Where a dispute proceeds beyond the CRA audit and objection stages to the Tax Court of Canada, litigation regularly hinges on the admissibility and weight of independent expert witness reports under the Tax Court of Canada Rules, as seen in Hypercube Inc. (2015 TCC) and 6379249 Canada Inc. (2015 TCC).
Conclusions and Strategic Compliance Recommendations

Canada's federal and provincial R&D tax incentive landscape presents a dual reality for corporate claimants in 2026: legislative reforms under federal Bill C-15 and Québec's March 2025 Budget have expanded expenditure caps, entity eligibility, and capital equipment coverage to historic highs, while federal appellate courts have reinforced strict adherence to the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria and contemporaneous record-keeping.

To optimize net cash recovery and ensure audit resilience, Canadian corporate claimants should execute five integrated compliance strategies. First, corporations must perform an annual quantitative comparison on Line 160 of Form T661 between the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount under Regulation 2900(4) and the Traditional Method, electing the Traditional Method whenever incremental cloud computing, GPU training, and utility overhead exceeds 55% of the eligible SR&ED salary base. Second, closely held CCPCs must structure founder and specified employee (≥10% shareholder) compensation using regular base salary (within the subsection 37(9.1) cap of 5 × YMPE, and 2.5 × YMPE for the proxy salary base) rather than dividends, bonuses, or profit-based pay, which are statutorily excluded from the SR&ED and proxy salary bases. Third, pre-profit Ontario startups should formally waive the non-refundable 3.5% ORDTC on Schedule T2SCH508 so that subsection 127(11.1) assistance reductions do not erode their 35% refundable federal SR&ED cash refund, and all claimants stacking direct grants (such as NRC IRAP or Regional AI Initiative funding) should allocate non-SR&ED commercial tasks to grant budgets wherever permissible. Fourth, enterprises acquiring R&D machinery or hardware on or after December 16, 2024, must maintain utilization logs demonstrating ≥ 90% SR&ED usage in Canada over the asset's useful life to capture the restored 35% federal ITC (40% refundable) and Québec's 30%/20% refundable CRIC. Finally, engineering and software teams must embed contemporaneous hypothesis-test-result logging directly into their project management and version-control workflows, ensuring an unbroken evidentiary chain capable of satisfying CRA Research and Technology Advisors and the Tax Court of Canada.
